chapters.title: Chapter 1 — Organizational Design Foundations
chapters.content_html:
Organizational Design

Definition

Organizational design is the deliberate process of structuring an organization’s roles, workflows, authority relationships, coordination systems, and cultural environment so that it can achieve its goals effectively.

Explanation

This course treats organizations as things that can be designed, not just inherited. Organizational design is about making choices: how work should be divided, who should make decisions, how communication should flow, how performance should be measured, and what behaviours should be encouraged. A well-designed organization aligns its structure, people, systems, and culture with what it is trying to accomplish. A poorly designed organization may still have talented people, but they will often work at cross-purposes, experience confusion, or struggle to respond to change.

A useful way to think about organizational design is that it sits between strategy and performance. Strategy says what the organization is trying to achieve. Organizational design determines whether the organization is actually set up to achieve it.

Framework components

Major design elements

  • Structure: levels of hierarchy, reporting relationships, departmentalization, span of control
  • Systems and processes: communication channels, workflows, decision processes, performance measurement
  • People: roles, required skills, staffing, training and development
  • Culture: values, norms, expected behaviours, patterns of collaboration

Example

A startup moving from ten people to one hundred people has to decide whether to stay informal or create defined teams, managers, hiring systems, and clearer decision rights. That is an organizational design problem.

Explanation

Why it matters

On an exam, organizational design is often the background logic behind a scenario. If a firm is struggling with slow decisions, weak coordination, low innovation, or role confusion, the real issue is often misaligned design.

Related concepts

Related concepts

organizational structure, goals, strategy, culture, coordination, decision-making

Why Organizations Matter

Explanation

Organizations matter because they dominate modern economic and social life, and because organizational structure can influence technical performance, quality, coordination, and innovation. The course repeatedly emphasizes that organizational problems are not separate from operational or technical problems. A poorly coordinated organization can produce slower decisions, weaker quality, and worse innovation even if the technical expertise inside it is strong.

Explanation

Why it matters

If a case looks like a technical failure, an exam question may still be asking you to identify an organizational-design problem underneath it.

Organization

Definition

An organization is a stable and interacting collection of individuals with a common and specific goal.

Explanation

The course definition emphasizes several attributes:

  • organizations are social entities, meaning people are central
  • they have distinct membership
  • they have structure, such as division of labour and coordination
  • they are relatively permanent
  • they aim at a common goal
  • they interact with the environment
  • they use technology

This matters because it distinguishes organizations from loose temporary groups. A random crowd is not an organization. A university, company, hospital, or charity is an organization.

Example

The University of Toronto qualifies as an organization because it has members, formal roles, hierarchy, goals, systems, and long-term continuity.

Explanation

Why it matters

When a question asks you to identify what makes organizations function effectively, you should think beyond “people working together” and mention structure, coordination, goals, and environment.

Organizational Theory

Definition

Organizational theory is a way of seeing and analyzing organizations more accurately and deeply.

Explanation

Organizational theory is not just a list of facts about organizations. It provides perspectives and frameworks that help explain why organizations look the way they do, why they behave differently, and why certain design choices create certain outcomes. The major point is that no single lens captures everything. Organizations are complex, and theory gives us multiple ways to interpret them.

Explanation

Why it matters

On exams, organizational theory shows up when you are asked to interpret a case, explain why a design choice makes sense, or compare older and newer ways of organizing work.

Related concepts

Related concepts

classical management, contemporary management, bureaucracy, collaboration, learning organizations

Classical Management

Definition

Classical management is an early perspective on organizations that treats them as systems that should be designed for efficiency, hierarchy, order, and control.

Explanation

Classical management assumes organizations work best when tasks are clearly defined, authority is formalized, and managers search for the best way to organize work. It is associated with bureaucracy and with the belief that there may be a single best method for performing a task. Classical management is especially useful in routine, stable, efficiency-oriented settings, but it becomes more problematic when work is complex, creative, or uncertain.

Two major branches from class are:

  • Scientific management: Frederick Taylor; focused on the shop floor and on designing work scientifically
  • Administrative principles: Henri Fayol; focused on how the organization as a whole should be managed

Example

An assembly-line environment with highly standardized tasks, clear supervision, and narrow roles reflects classical management assumptions.

Explanation

Why it matters

Many exam scenarios ask you to identify when a structure is overly rigid, too bureaucratic, or overly efficiency-driven. That often traces back to classical management logic.

Related concepts

Related concepts

scientific management, administrative principles, bureaucracy, mechanistic structure

Scientific Management

Definition

Scientific management is a branch of classical management that argues work should be designed through precise study in order to maximize efficiency.

Explanation

Taylor’s view was that organizations should analyze tasks scientifically and then determine the best way to perform them. This usually involves:

  • standard procedures
  • selecting workers with the right abilities
  • training workers in those procedures
  • careful planning by management
  • incentives tied to output

The key assumption is that management does the thinking and workers execute standardized tasks.

Example

The Bethlehem Steel example captures this logic: management studies the task, sets precise expectations, and uses incentives to increase productivity.

Explanation

Why it matters

You should know both the strengths and limits. Scientific management can improve efficiency in routine work, but it can also reduce autonomy, creativity, and worker ownership. It is often a poor fit for knowledge work.

Explanation

Scenario-style question

A firm wants to maximize routine output in a stable production environment by carefully specifying each step of work. Which concept best explains this design choice?

Administrative Principles

Definition

Administrative principles are broad management principles focused on designing and managing the organization as a whole.

Explanation

Unlike scientific management, which focuses on task execution, administrative principles address questions like authority, unity, coordination, discipline, centralization, and overall management structure. Fayol’s framework is foundational because it shaped how managers think about hierarchy and formal design.

Framework components

Fayol’s principles you should especially know

  • division of work
  • authority and responsibility
  • discipline
  • unity of command
  • unity of direction
  • subordination of individual interests to the general interest
  • remuneration
  • centralization
  • scalar chain
  • order
  • equity
  • stability of tenure
  • initiative
  • esprit de corps

Fayol’s contribution matters because he moved beyond the shop floor and focused on management of the organization as a whole. Scientific management asks how tasks should be done efficiently. Administrative principles ask how authority, coordination, unity, discipline, and organization-wide management should be designed.

Explanation

Why it matters

Even if an exam does not ask you to list all fourteen principles, it may ask you to recognize them in a scenario, such as unity of command, centralization, or division of work.

Hawthorne Studies

Definition

The Hawthorne studies are associated with a shift away from purely mechanical views of organizations and toward greater attention to social and human dimensions of work.

Explanation

The major importance of the Hawthorne studies in this course is not memorizing every experimental detail. It is understanding that they helped move organization theory away from the assumption that efficiency alone explains performance. Informal relationships, motivation, attention, and social dynamics also matter.

Explanation

Why it matters

This is part of the historical bridge between classical management and more contemporary attention to people, communication, and informal organization.

Contemporary Management

Definition

Contemporary management views organizations as more decentralized, adaptive, collaborative, and information-dependent than classical management did.

Explanation

Contemporary management recognizes that many modern organizations operate in uncertain environments, depend on knowledge sharing, and require flexibility rather than rigid control. Instead of assuming one best way, it emphasizes fit, context, learning, adaptability, and communication.

Related concepts

Contrast with classical management

  • Classical management emphasizes control, standardization, and hierarchy
  • Contemporary management emphasizes collaboration, adaptability, and information sharing

Classical management is most comfortable in stable settings where efficiency and routine performance matter most. Contemporary management is more useful when organizations face uncertainty, rapid change, knowledge work, and the need for learning across functions.

Example

A cross-functional product team in a software company is usually better explained by contemporary management than by classical management.

Explanation

Why it matters

Comparison questions often ask you to contrast classical and contemporary views of organizing. This is a high-value relationship to know.

Organizational Structure

Definition

Organizational structure is the sum of the ways an organization divides labour into distinct tasks and then achieves coordination among them.

Explanation

This Mintzberg definition is foundational because it links two major design problems: how work is split up and how those separate pieces are brought back together. A good structure is not just an org chart; it is a system for specialization and coordination.

Explanation

Why it matters

Many scenario questions ask you to infer structure from evidence about task division, reporting relationships, coordination, or decision-making.

Five Design Variables

Explanation

The five major design variables are:

  1. Division of Labour (specialization)

The way labour is divided into distinct tasks.

  • Benefit: expert performance, less training time, less dependence on any one person for all tasks
  • Downside: more coordination required, possible worker alienation
  1. Collaboration

Working together through communication, coordination, and cooperation.

  1. Shape

The height of the hierarchy and span of control.

  • Tall/narrow structures allow closer supervision but can slow communication
  • Shallow/broad structures reduce hierarchy but can disconnect managers from detail
  1. Decision-Making (centralization)

The level of hierarchy with authority to make decisions.

  • Centralized: more consistency, less flexibility
  • Decentralized: better use of expertise, less consistency
  1. Grouping of Tasks

The structural configuration used to group work.

  • Functional
  • Divisional
  • Matrix

Why it matters

This is one of the most exam-relevant frameworks in the course. Scenario questions often ask which design variable should change.

The 3 C’s of Collaboration

Explanation

Communication

Information exchange.

Explanation

Coordination

Aligning tasks, responsibilities, and timing.

Explanation

Cooperation

Willingness to work together toward a shared goal.

Why it matters

If a scenario describes departments not sharing updates, duplicated work, or people withholding effort, the issue may lie in one of the 3 C’s.

Mintzberg’s Five Coordination Mechanisms

Explanation

  1. Mutual adjustment — informal communication among people doing interdependent work
  2. Direct supervision — one person coordinates others by giving instructions
  3. Standardization of work processes — tasks are coordinated by specifying how work should be done
  4. Standardization of outputs — tasks are coordinated by specifying required results
  5. Standardization of skills — tasks are coordinated because people are trained to perform in predictable ways

Why it matters

If the case says everyone follows the same SOP, think standardization of work processes. If the case says a professional license or degree ensures consistent work, think standardization of skills.

Grouping of Tasks — Structural Forms

Explanation

Functional structure

Grouped by job function such as marketing, finance, or operations.

Explanation

Why it matters

Functional structure is good for specialization and efficiency, but it can also create silos.

Explanation

Divisional structure

Grouped by product, market, or region.

Explanation

Why it matters

Divisional structure is good for responsiveness and focus, but it can duplicate resources.

Explanation

Matrix structure

Employees belong to both a functional and divisional grouping.

Explanation

Why it matters

Matrix structure is good for sharing expertise and flexibility, but it can create role conflict and dual-authority tension.

Vertical vs Horizontal Information Linkages

Explanation

Vertical information linkages

Coordinate activities between top and bottom of an organization and are designed for control. Examples include hierarchy, rules, plans, and vertical information systems.

Explanation

Horizontal information linkages

Overcome barriers between departments and are designed for collaboration. Examples include direct contact, task forces, full-time integrators, and cross-functional teams.

Why it matters

A common exam move is asking whether a company needs more vertical or horizontal communication.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — Mission, Vision, Goals, and Strategy
chapters.nav_title: Chapter 2 — Mission, Vision, Goals, and Strategy
chapters.content_html:
Mission

Definition

Mission is the official goal of an organization. It describes the organization’s reason for being, its scope, and what it is trying to accomplish.

Explanation

A mission statement is broad and high-level. It communicates what the organization exists to do and often includes values and beliefs as well. Mission statements are usually somewhat stable over time and are often used for legitimacy, identity, and public communication rather than for daily task guidance.

Example

A hospital foundation’s mission may focus on improving the lives of children and families through investment in health and scientific advances.

Explanation

Why it matters

Mission is often tested through comparison. You need to know that mission is official and broad, not the same thing as a short-term measurable target.

Related concepts

Related concepts

vision, official goals, operative goals, legitimacy

Vision

Definition

Vision describes the envisioned future of the organization — what it aspires to become or what change it wants to create.

Explanation

Vision is more future-oriented and aspirational than mission. It often captures the organization’s ideal future state and can be ambitious or even “wild.” Unlike mission, which focuses on the organization’s purpose, vision focuses on where the organization is trying to go.

Explanation

Why it matters

A common exam move is to ask you to distinguish mission from vision or explain how they differ in purpose.

Related concepts

Related concepts

Mission is about what the organization is and does now, or why it exists. Vision is about the desired future and what the organization aspires to become or create.

Organizational Values

Definition

Organizational values are the beliefs and standards that guide how the organization behaves and makes decisions.

Explanation

Values help shape culture, priorities, and tradeoffs. They are often stated alongside mission and vision, but their real importance comes from whether they influence actual choices.

Official Goals

Definition

Official goals are the formally stated goals of the organization, usually captured in mission and vision statements.

Explanation

Official goals are deliberately broad, externally visible, and often somewhat vague. They help create legitimacy, align identity, and communicate values to stakeholders. They are not especially useful for daily operating decisions because they are usually not specific or measurable enough.

Explanation

Why it matters

Official goals are broad and public-facing; operative goals are the more concrete goals that guide actual daily decisions.

Operative Goals

Definition

Operative goals are the actual, specific, measurable outcomes an organization tries to achieve through its operating procedures.

Explanation

Operative goals translate broad purpose into actionable targets. They relate closely to what the organization is really trying to do in practice. The lecture emphasized several categories:

  • resources
  • market
  • employee development
  • innovation and change
  • productivity
  • overall performance

Explanation

Why it matters

Operative goals are much more likely to drive actual organizational design choices, such as adding units, changing decision rights, investing in training, or redesigning workflows.

Official goals help communicate purpose and legitimacy. Operative goals explain what the organization is actually trying to accomplish in practice.

Effectiveness and Efficiency

Explanation

Effectiveness

The degree to which the organization achieves its goals.

Explanation

Efficiency

The amount of resources used to achieve those goals.

Explanation

An organization can be efficient without being effective, or effective without being efficient. Effectiveness asks whether the right outcomes are achieved. Efficiency asks how economically the organization achieves them.

Explanation

Why it matters

Organizations may say they value effectiveness and efficiency, but they still need ways to measure goal attainment. Different goals may be easier or harder to measure depending on whether they are concrete, short-term, qualitative, or aspirational.

Goal Conflict

Definition

Goal conflict occurs when different goals are in tension so that improving one makes another harder to achieve.

Explanation

Organizations have many stakeholders and many priorities. Market goals, employee goals, safety goals, innovation goals, and performance goals can conflict. Departments can also conflict with each other.

Explanation

Challenges of goal setting

  • goals may be vague or too broad
  • multiple goals can conflict
  • short-term measurable goals can crowd out long-term priorities
  • units may pursue local goals rather than organization-wide goals

Goal Displacement

Definition

Goal displacement occurs when the means used to achieve a goal become the goal themselves.

Explanation

The class used means-end inversion to explain this. Rules and procedures that were originally supposed to help the organization become so important that following them becomes more important than achieving the original goal.

Example

In bureaucracy, a company may become more focused on not breaking procedures than on serving customers effectively.

Explanation

Means-ends inversion

Means-ends inversion occurs when processes, rules, or measures that were supposed to help achieve goals become goals in themselves.

Explanation

Why it matters

This is closely related to goal displacement and is useful in diagnosing dysfunctional organizations.

Strategy

Definition

Strategy is the plan for interacting with the competitive environment in order to achieve organizational goals.

Explanation

Goals tell us where the organization wants to go; strategy explains how it plans to get there. Different strategies require different design choices. A low-cost strategy often pushes toward efficiency and standardization, while an innovation-oriented strategy often pushes toward flexibility and collaboration.

Miles and Snow Strategy Typology

Explanation

Prospector

Seeks opportunities, innovation, and exploration.

  • performs well in dynamic environments
  • more flexible, decentralized, and organic structures

Explanation

Defender

Focuses on efficiency, stability, and protecting a secure market position.

  • emphasizes efficiency and control
  • more centralized and mechanistic structures

Explanation

Analyzer

Maintains a stable core while selectively innovating.

  • balances stability in some areas with innovation in others
  • often uses mixed structural arrangements

Explanation

Reactor

Lacks a consistent strategy and responds inconsistently.

  • often shows poor fit between environment, strategy, and structure

Porter’s Competitive Strategies

Explanation

Low-cost leadership

Compete by being the lowest-cost producer.

This requires efficiency, standardization, cost control, and often more formalization.

Explanation

Differentiation

Compete by offering something unique.

This requires creativity, responsiveness, and often more flexibility.

Explanation

Focused low-cost

Low-cost strategy in a narrow segment.

Explanation

Focused differentiation

Differentiation in a narrow segment.

Focused strategy targets a narrow segment. Structure depends on whether the focus is cost or uniqueness, but generally requires tight alignment with customer needs.

How Goals Drive Organizational Design

Explanation

Goals influence:

  • division of labour
  • collaboration
  • organizational shape
  • centralization
  • grouping of tasks

A strong innovation goal may push toward flatter structure and rapid decisions. A productivity goal may push toward standardization and stronger control.

Innovation goals often push toward flatter structure, faster decision-making, and investment in R&D. Productivity goals often push toward standardization, specialization, and tighter coordination. Employee development goals can push toward training, supervision, and safer processes. Market goals often push toward efficiency, customer focus, and growth-supporting structures.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — Organizational Technology and Lifecycle
chapters.content_html:
Organizational Technology

Definition

Organizational technology refers to the tools, techniques, processes, and work methods an organization uses to transform inputs into outputs.

Explanation

In this course, “technology” does not just mean digital tools or machines. It includes the underlying production process: how work gets done. Technology matters because different kinds of work require different structures, coordination patterns, and decision systems. A routine mass-production system needs a different organization from a research lab or a consulting team.

Explanation

Why it matters

A classic exam question is to link a type of technology to an appropriate structure.

Explanation

Core technology

Core technology is the work process directly related to the organization’s mission.

Examples:

  • university: teaching
  • health clinic: medical services
  • delivery company: sorting and package-delivery systems

Explanation

Noncore technology

Noncore technology refers to work processes that are not directly related to the primary mission but are still necessary to support the organization.

Examples:

  • HR
  • accounting
  • marketing
  • quality control
  • R&D

Explanation

Why it matters

Core technology strongly influences the structure of the technical core, while noncore departments should not automatically be organized the same way as the core. Their structure depends on task variety and analyzability.

Woodward’s Technology Types

Explanation

Small-Batch Production

Customized or low-volume production, often tailored to specific customer needs.

Explanation

Likely structural implications

  • lower formalization
  • more decentralized decisions
  • greater reliance on communication and expertise
  • more adaptability

Explanation

Mass Production

Standardized, high-volume production of identical products.

Explanation

Likely structural implications

  • high specialization
  • high formalization
  • centralization
  • stronger supervision
  • clear rules and routines

Explanation

Continuous-Process Production

Highly automated production that runs continuously through technical systems.

Explanation

Likely structural implications

  • high technical sophistication
  • skilled employees
  • strong coordination
  • more need for expertise-based responses

Explanation

Woodward’s findings

Mass production tended to be the most mechanistic. Small-batch and continuous-process work often required more flexibility and skilled adaptation than students intuitively expect.

Task Variety and Analyzability

Explanation

Task variety

Task variety is the frequency of unexpected and novel events in the work process.

  • low variety = repetitive, predictable work
  • high variety = frequent exceptions and new situations

Explanation

Analyzability

Analyzability is the degree to which work can be reduced to known mechanical steps and procedures.

  • high analyzability = clear procedures exist
  • low analyzability = judgment and interpretation are required

Explanation

Departmental Technology Categories

Explanation

Routine

  • low variety, high analyzability
  • example: clerical work, auditing
  • tends toward mechanistic structure

Explanation

Craft

  • low variety, low analyzability
  • example: fine-goods manufacturing, trades
  • often moderately organic

Explanation

Engineering

  • high variety, high analyzability
  • example: legal, accounting, or engineering work using known methods on varying cases
  • often more structured than nonroutine work

Explanation

Nonroutine

  • high variety, low analyzability
  • example: strategic planning, research, biotechnology
  • tends toward more organic structure

Technology and Structure

Explanation

More routine, repetitive work tends to fit mechanistic design. More uncertain, complex, customized work tends to fit organic design.

Related concepts

Service vs Manufacturing

Service technology

  • intangible output
  • simultaneous production and consumption
  • human contact is important
  • often labour- and knowledge-intensive
  • technical core employees are close to customers
  • often lower formalization and more decentralization

Manufacturing technology

  • tangible output
  • product can often be stored before consumption
  • more capital-intensive
  • direct customer contact is usually lower in the technical core
  • often more formalization, especially in mass production

Service organizations often require technical-core employees to be close to customers, which makes interpersonal and communication skill more important. Manufacturing work can often be separated from customers more easily than service work.

Workflow Interdependence

Definition

Workflow interdependence is the extent to which departments depend on one another for resources or materials to accomplish their tasks.

Explanation

Why it matters

Higher interdependence increases coordination needs and affects structure, communication, and control systems.

Organizational Lifecycle

Definition

Organizational lifecycle refers to the stages organizations tend to move through as they grow and become more complex over time.

Explanation

  • entrepreneurial
  • collectivity
  • formalization
  • elaboration

Explanation

Entrepreneurial stage

Founder control, low specialization, informal communication.

  • structure: simple, centralized, informal
  • control and reward systems: personal oversight rather than formal systems
  • innovation pattern: high experimentation
  • management style: founder-driven
  • central crisis: need for leadership

Explanation

Collectivity stage

Growth, stronger commitment, some specialization, still relatively informal.

  • structure: growing but still relatively informal
  • control and reward systems: stronger commitment with limited formal systems
  • innovation pattern: continued growth and expansion
  • management style: charismatic and relational
  • central crisis: need for delegation with control

Explanation

Formalization stage

More hierarchy, more procedures, clearer roles, more control.

  • structure: more hierarchy and standardization
  • control and reward systems: formal systems, budgets, procedures, and clearer accountability
  • innovation pattern: often slows as control increases
  • management style: professionalized administration
  • central crisis: red-tape crisis

Explanation

Elaboration stage

Complex organization using teams and adaptive systems to remain effective.

  • structure: complex, differentiated, and often team-based
  • control and reward systems: more sophisticated coordination and control systems
  • innovation pattern: must be deliberately revitalized
  • management style: collaborative and adaptive
  • central crisis: need for revitalization

Explanation

Why it matters

As organizations grow, structures that worked earlier may stop working.

chapters.title: Chapter 4.1 — Bureaucracy
chapters.content_html:
Bureaucracy

Definition

Bureaucracy is an organizational framework marked by rules and procedures, specialization and division of labour, hierarchy of authority, technically qualified personnel, separation of position and person, and written communications and records.

Explanation

Bureaucracy is often treated negatively in everyday language, but in organizational design it is a real structural form with both advantages and drawbacks. Bureaucracy exists because large organizations need consistency, accountability, predictability, and coordination across many people.

Explanation

  • reliability and consistency
  • coordination at scale
  • fairness and procedural consistency
  • role clarity

Bureaucracy can also support legitimacy, survival, and lower failure risk in many settings because it creates predictability, documentation, and formal accountability. In some contexts, clear rules can also reduce arbitrariness and offer protections for marginalized workers.

Explanation

Downsides

  • slower information flow
  • information dilution
  • reduced creativity and flexibility
  • cost
  • goal displacement risk

Explanation

Why Bureaucracy Persists

People may dislike bureaucracy, but it persists because large organizations need predictability, documentation, coordination, and legitimacy. Bureaucracy is not just red tape. It is a way of making large-scale organized action possible.

Mechanistic Structure

Explanation

A rigid structure characterized by high formalization, centralization, and hierarchy.

Explanation

Why it matters

Mechanistic structure is closely associated with bureaucracy and is usually a better fit when consistency, predictability, and control matter more than flexibility.

Organic Structure

Explanation

A flexible structure characterized by lower formalization, greater decentralization, and stronger lateral communication.

Explanation

Why it matters

Organic structure is usually a better fit when the organization needs responsiveness, adaptation, and more fluid communication.

Breaking into Smaller Units

Explanation

One redesign move is to preserve some organizational control while creating smaller units or microenterprises that can respond more quickly. This approach tries to reduce bureaucratic sluggishness without eliminating coordination entirely.

chapters.title: Chapter 4.2 — Organizational Culture
chapters.content_html:
Organizational Culture

Definition

Organizational culture is the set of values, norms, guiding beliefs, and understandings shared by members of an organization and taught to new members.

Explanation

Culture shapes how people interpret situations, what behaviour they see as acceptable, how they communicate, and how they understand the organization's identity. Culture is partly visible and partly hidden.

Levels of Culture

Explanation

  • observable culture: symbols, stories, language, and rites or ceremonies that people can see directly
  • deeper culture: less visible assumptions, values, and beliefs that shape how people interpret and behave

Explanation

Why it matters

An exam case may show only visible clues, while the real issue lies in deeper assumptions and values.

Culture Emergence

Explanation

Culture emerges both naturally and through intentional shaping by leaders and organizational practices. It grows through repeated behaviour, shared experiences, and what the organization rewards or tolerates.

Functions of Culture

Related concepts

Internal integration

Culture helps members develop a collective identity and understand how to work together.

Related concepts

External integration

Culture influences how the organization responds to customers, competitors, and the external environment.

Four Cultural Indicators

Explanation

The lecture highlights four cultural indicators that help diagnose culture:

  • rites and ceremonies
  • stories
  • symbols
  • language

Rites and Ceremonies

Explanation

Rites and ceremonies are visible events or practices that communicate what the organization values, who belongs, and what kinds of behaviour are celebrated.

Framework components

Types of rites and ceremonies

  • passage
  • enhancement
  • renewal
  • integration

Explanation

Why it matters

Rites and ceremonies are useful diagnostic tools because they show what the organization publicly recognizes, rewards, and reinforces.

Stories

Explanation

Stories communicate lessons about what the organization admires, condemns, remembers, or expects. Stories often carry the culture by showing what happened to people who acted in certain ways and what those outcomes meant.

Explanation

Why it matters

If a story is repeatedly told, it often signals a deeper cultural message about risk, loyalty, customer service, hierarchy, or success.

Symbols

Explanation

Symbols are visible objects, arrangements, or cues that communicate cultural meaning. They can include office layout, dress, status markers, physical space, or visible signals about who matters and what is valued.

Explanation

Why it matters

Symbols are useful because they reveal culture even when nobody states the values directly.

Language

Explanation

Language includes the special words, phrases, labels, and ways of speaking that members use inside the organization.

Explanation

Why it matters

Language signals what the organization treats as normal, important, desirable, or unacceptable. It can also show who belongs and who does not.

Culture Strength

Explanation

Strong culture means values are widely shared and internalized. Weak culture means there is less consensus and less behavioural guidance across members.

Explanation

Why it matters

A strong culture can create alignment, but it can also make change harder if the shared assumptions are deeply entrenched.

Subcultures

Explanation

Different teams or units can develop their own cultures within the same organization. Departments, occupations, or locations may not all interpret the organization in the same way.

Explanation

Implications

  • Subcultures can improve local coordination because people in the same area develop shared norms.
  • Subcultures can support performance when the local culture fits the work well.
  • Subcultures can also create misunderstanding, conflict, or coordination problems when units develop very different assumptions and priorities.

Explanation

Why it matters

When departments clash despite being in the same organization, subcultures may explain the conflict better than personality differences alone.

Cultural Embeddedness

Definition

Cultural embeddedness is the degree to which an individual internalizes the organization's culture and accepts group norms.

Explanation

Benefits of fitting in

  • easier understanding of expectations
  • smoother coordination with others
  • stronger sense of belonging

Explanation

Consequences of fitting in too strongly

Strong cultural embeddedness can support coordination, but it can also reduce questioning or make change harder if people become deeply attached to existing norms.

Structural Embeddedness

Explanation

Structural embeddedness is how well an individual fits into the organization's communication and collaboration network.

Explanation

Why it matters

Cultural embeddedness is about fit with norms and values. Structural embeddedness is about fit with the actual pattern of communication and relationships.

chapters.title: Chapter 5.1 — Interorganizational Relationships
chapters.content_html:
Interorganizational Relationships

Definition

Interorganizational relationships are relatively enduring resource transactions, flows, and linkages that occur among two or more organizations.

Explanation

Organizations do not operate in isolation. They interact with suppliers, customers, competitors, regulators, associations, and partners. These relationships allow organizations to pursue mutual interests while remaining independent and autonomous.

Organizational Ecosystems

Explanation

An organizational ecosystem is a system formed by interacting organizations and their environment.

Why Interorganizational Relationships Matter

Explanation

  • organizations learn from observing others
  • they import practices and routines
  • they gain access to resources and knowledge
  • strategy can depend on relationships with other organizations

Motivations for Cooperation

Explanation

  • fast, effective learning
  • cost savings
  • economies of scale
  • specialization benefits
  • reduction of risk and uncertainty
  • reputation enhancement through association

Four Types

Explanation

Alliances

Voluntarily initiated enduring relationships involving coordination, resource sharing, or co-development.

Explanation

Consortia

Relationships in which multiple organizations collaborate around a shared project, capability, or industry objective.

Explanation

Joint ventures

A separate jointly controlled arrangement created by two or more organizations.

Explanation

Long-term sourcing agreements

Relatively enduring supply relationships used to secure inputs, coordinate activity, and reduce uncertainty.

Interorganizational Framework

Explanation

Relationships between organizations can be assessed by:

  • their degree of similarity
  • their degree of competitiveness versus cooperativeness

This matters because different theories become more useful depending on whether organizations are similar or dissimilar, and whether they are competing or cooperating.

Resource Dependence Theory

Explanation

Resource Dependence Theory explains how organizations manage dependence on external resources.

It assumes organizations try to reduce vulnerability by securing access to important resources and increasing their control over supply conditions.

Explanation

What determines dependence

  1. The importance of the resource to the organization
  2. The amount of discretion or monopoly power held by those who control the resource

Explanation

Why it matters

This theory is especially useful when firms cooperate because another organization controls something essential.

Population Ecology Perspective

Explanation

A perspective explaining diversity and adaptation across populations of organizations.

Explanation

Population ecology argues that environments select organizational forms. Not all forms survive. New organizational forms emerge to fit new niches, and change across a population often happens more through the birth of new forms than through deep reform of old ones.

Explanation

Why it matters

Niche logic matters. A form that fits one environment may fail in another, and older organizations may be less likely to change than new ones are to emerge.

Collaborative Networks

Explanation

Collaborative networks involve organizations partnering with other organizations or suppliers to create mutual value.

Explanation

Why Collaborative Networks Matter

  • they help share risk when entering new markets
  • they reduce costs
  • they can improve innovation and problem solving
  • they can help firms enter global markets
  • they can add value to both parties

Institutionalism

Explanation

Institutionalism explains how organizations become similar because they seek legitimacy.

Explanation

Organizations are influenced by stakeholder expectations and by the broader environment’s norms and beliefs. They may borrow structures and practices from other organizations not because those practices are most efficient, but because they are seen as proper, credible, or legitimate.

chapters.title: Chapter 5.2 — Communication
chapters.content_html:
Communication in Organizations

Definition

Communication in organizations is the social process through which information, meaning, and understanding move among individuals and groups.

Explanation

Communication is affected by differences in knowledge, hierarchy, power, and organizational structure. It is not just about passing messages; it enables coordination, control, and collaboration.

Vertical Information Linkages

Explanation

Communication systems coordinating activities between the top and bottom of the organization. They are designed mainly for control.

Explanation

  • hierarchical referral
  • rules and plans
  • vertical information systems
  • formal reporting

Horizontal Information Linkages

Explanation

Communication systems coordinating across departments or units. They are designed more for collaboration than control.

Explanation

  • information systems
  • direct contact / liaison roles
  • task forces
  • integrators
  • cross-functional teams

Upward Communication

Explanation

Communication from lower levels to higher levels.

It is often filtered or selectively positive. Employees may share information upward while softening bad news or withholding problems.

Downward Communication

Explanation

Communication from managers to subordinates about goals, policies, task instructions, and feedback.

Upward Voice

Explanation

Employees’ willingness and ability to communicate concerns, ideas, and problems upward.

Upward communication is information moving upward. Upward voice is more intentional and involves employees actively raising concerns, ideas, or challenges in hopes of improving the organization.

Framework components

Forms

Upward voice can be formal through suggestion systems, grievance procedures, or unions, or informal through ordinary conversations and direct manager interaction.

Explanation

Benefits of Upward Voice to the Organization

  • better problem detection
  • improved learning
  • better decisions
  • stronger ethical correction

Explanation

Benefits of Upward Voice to Employees

  • more agency
  • more psychological safety
  • a stronger sense of respect and inclusion

Explanation

Consequences of Silence

  • problems remain hidden longer
  • decisions become worse
  • ethical issues can persist
  • frustration and disengagement grow

Explanation

Structural Enablers of Upward Voice

  • proximity to leaders
  • fewer hierarchical layers
  • parallel communication channels
  • technology-enabled mechanisms
  • formal suggestion or grievance systems
  • leader behaviour that invites input

Explanation

Leader Humor and Upward Voice

Leader behaviour, including humour, can sometimes reduce status barriers, improve relationships, and make employees more willing to speak up.

Explanation

Extreme Voice / Radical Transparency

Some organizations experiment with unusually direct voice cultures in which speaking up is expected almost constantly. This pushes the idea of upward voice to an extreme and raises questions about whether radical transparency is always desirable.

Media Richness Logic

Explanation

Communication media differ in how much feedback, clarification, nuance, and interpersonal cue-reading they support.

Explanation

Richer media

Richer media are more appropriate when a message is ambiguous, sensitive, controversial, or emotionally significant because they make clarification easier and allow more immediate feedback.

Explanation

Leaner media

Leaner media are often sufficient for routine, standardized, or low-ambiguity messages that do not require much interpretation.

Explanation

Why it matters

If an organization is communicating a routine update, a leaner medium may work well. If it is communicating a major change or trying to build understanding around uncertainty, richer communication is usually more appropriate.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — Innovation
chapters.content_html:
Innovation

Definition

Innovation is the adoption or development of new ideas, products, services, processes, or ways of organizing that improve how the organization functions or competes.

Explanation

Innovation is not just about having ideas. It also requires structures, collaboration, leadership, and culture that allow ideas to be developed, adopted, and implemented. A team can generate ideas and still fail to innovate if the organization does not create the conditions to support implementation.

Innovation = Creativity + Informed Craft + Organization-level Considerations

Explanation

The lecture frames innovation as:

Innovation = Creativity + Informed Craft + Organization-level considerations

Explanation

Creativity

Creativity is the generation of novel and useful ideas. It matters because organizations need ideas that are not only different, but also relevant and potentially valuable.

Explanation

Informed Craft

Informed craft means the knowledge, judgment, and skill needed to turn a raw idea into something workable. Creativity alone is not enough if the idea cannot be refined, adapted, tested, or executed well.

Explanation

Organization-level considerations

Organization-level considerations include the structural and cultural conditions that determine whether ideas can actually move forward. These include support, coordination, leadership, resources, implementation capacity, and willingness to change.

Explanation

Why it matters

This formula is exam-relevant because it helps explain why a creative organization may still fail to innovate. The missing piece may be craft, or it may be the organizational conditions needed for adoption and implementation.

Innovation vs Creativity

Explanation

Creativity is the generation of novel and useful ideas. Innovation is the implementation or adoption of those ideas in organizational practice.

Explanation

Why it matters

A team can be creative without being innovative if it generates interesting ideas that are never adopted or implemented.

What Can Change?

Explanation

  • product or service
  • strategy and structure
  • culture
  • technology

Explanation

Why it matters

Innovation is not limited to products. A firm can innovate through technology, organizational design, culture, or strategy as well.

Elements for Successful Change and Innovation

Explanation

The lecture highlights several elements that help ideas become real organizational change:

Explanation

Ideas

Innovation begins with ideas. Without ideas, there is nothing to develop or implement.

Explanation

Needs

Ideas are more likely to be adopted when they are tied to a real organizational or market need. A technically interesting idea may still fail if people do not see why it matters.

Explanation

Adoption

Adoption is the point at which the organization agrees to take up the new idea. This is different from generating the idea. An idea can exist for a long time without being accepted.

Explanation

Implementation

Implementation is the process of turning the adopted idea into actual practice. Many organizations struggle here: they approve change in principle but fail to redesign roles, routines, systems, or behaviour to make it work.

Explanation

Resources

Innovation needs resources such as time, funding, people, attention, and managerial support. Even strong ideas can fail if the organization does not back them with real capacity.

Explanation

Why it matters

These elements are useful in cases because they help diagnose where innovation is breaking down. The problem may not be creativity. It may be weak adoption, weak implementation, or lack of resources.

Culture of Change

Definition

Culture of change refers to organizational norms and expectations that support adaptation, experimentation, and openness to new ideas.

Explanation

A culture of change does not mean constant chaos. It means that change is treated as something the organization can discuss, test, and work through rather than automatically resist. In that kind of culture, people are more willing to question routines, propose alternatives, and participate in implementation.

Explanation

Why it matters

An organization may say it wants innovation while still having a culture that punishes experimentation or treats deviation as a problem. In a case, this shows misalignment between stated goals and the actual culture of change.

Risk Management in Innovation and Change

Definition

Risk management in innovation means recognizing that new ideas involve uncertainty and creating ways to evaluate, contain, and learn from that uncertainty.

Explanation

Organizations do not support innovation by eliminating all risk. They support it by managing risk intelligently. This can include staged testing, review, learning from failure, and making sure risks are visible rather than hidden. If people believe every failed attempt will be punished, they are less likely to experiment or speak up.

Explanation

Why it matters

When a scenario shows fear of failure, overreaction to experiments, or reluctance to test new ideas, the problem may be weak risk management rather than lack of creativity.

Resources and Infrastructure

Definition

Resources and infrastructure are the organizational supports that make innovation possible in practice.

Explanation

Resources include time, money, staffing, and managerial attention. Infrastructure includes systems, processes, communication channels, and spaces for coordination and development. Innovation is harder when people are expected to innovate on top of overloaded jobs without time, support, or implementation pathways.

Explanation

Why it matters

If a company talks about innovation but does not provide time, budget, decision support, or implementation systems, the issue is not motivation alone. It is missing resources and infrastructure.

Principles of Creativity

Explanation

  1. Look for the next right answer
  2. Diversify your viewpoints
  3. Defer all judgment
  4. Challenge your assumptions
  5. Give yourself time to be creative

Looking for the next right answer matters because people often stop too early and accept the first workable idea. Diversifying viewpoints matters because shifting perspective can reveal options that are invisible from a single angle. Deferring judgment matters because early evaluation can shut down idea generation. Challenging assumptions matters because hidden assumptions often block better solutions. Giving yourself time matters because creative work often improves when people are not forced to accept the first acceptable answer immediately.

Innovation as a Group-Level Process

Explanation

Three levers

  1. structure
  2. collaboration
  3. leadership

Explanation

Innovation depends not only on individual creativity, but also on whether the organization creates the conditions to support adoption, coordination, and implementation. Structure affects who can decide and who must coordinate. Collaboration affects whether ideas move across boundaries. Leadership affects whether people feel encouraged to try new approaches and keep developing them.

Explanation

Why it matters

If a case shows that good ideas are trapped inside one team, blocked by hierarchy, or unsupported by leaders, the issue is at the group or organization level rather than the individual level.

Transactional vs Transformational Leadership

Explanation

Transactional leadership

Transactional leadership relies on exchange, monitoring, rewards, and correction. It is more useful when an organization wants reliable performance within an existing system.

Explanation

Transformational leadership

Transformational leadership focuses on inspiring employees to create change that supports the future success of the organization.

Explanation

Why it matters

Transactional leadership is usually a better fit when the organization wants routine compliance, consistency, and control. Transformational leadership is more useful when the organization is trying to support change, adaptation, and innovation.

Psychological Safety

Definition

Psychological safety is a climate in which employees feel safe taking interpersonal risks, such as sharing ideas or asking questions.

Explanation

Psychological safety supports innovation because people are more likely to ask questions, admit uncertainty, propose ideas, and speak up about concerns when they do not expect embarrassment or punishment for doing so.

Explanation

What it is not

  • mere comfort
  • lack of accountability
  • universal agreement

Explanation

Why it matters

If people stay silent, avoid experimentation, or hide concerns because they fear punishment, the organization is missing psychological safety. That weakens both learning and innovation.

chapters.title: Chapter 8.1 — Change Management
chapters.content_html:
Organizational Change

Definition

Organizational change is the adoption of a new idea or behaviour by an organization.

Explanation

Change may involve structure, technology, culture, strategy, processes, or roles. The course distinguishes change from innovation: innovation is something new to the industry, market, or broader environment, while change is new to the organization itself.

Framework components

Domains of change

The lecture treats four domains as especially important:

  • technology
  • product and service
  • strategy and structure
  • culture

These domains are interdependent. A change in one often creates pressure for change in another.

Explanation

Why it matters

If a case shows one change producing ripple effects elsewhere, the exam point is often that the domains of change are interconnected rather than isolated.

Incremental Change

Explanation

Builds on existing norms and practices.

This is also called nondivergent change because it does not break sharply from existing assumptions and practices.

Radical Change

Explanation

Involves dramatic shifts in values or practices that had previously been taken for granted.

This is also called divergent change because it breaks more sharply from previously taken-for-granted assumptions or practices.

Change vs Innovation

Explanation

Change is new to the organization. Innovation is new to the industry, market, or broader environment.

Resistance to Change

Explanation

Opposition, discomfort, or reluctance in response to organizational change.

Resistance can come from structural barriers, cultural attachment, power loss, uncertainty, status concerns, and identity threats. Employees may not just dislike change in general. They may see a change as threatening competence, relationships, routines, or status.

Explanation

Why people fear sudden change

  • uncertainty about outcomes
  • fear of loss
  • disruption of routines
  • threat to identity or competence
  • lack of control

Factors That Make Change Harder

Explanation

  • structural processes such as bureaucracy or many approval steps
  • structural limits on foresight when senior decision-makers are far from frontline realities
  • cultural opposition to the change

Kotter’s Change Framework

Explanation

Most important steps to know:

  • establish urgency
  • build a guiding coalition
  • create a vision
  • communicate the vision
  • empower action
  • create short-term wins
  • consolidate gains
  • anchor change in culture

Explanation

Why transformations fail

  • not creating enough urgency
  • weak guiding coalition
  • underpowered vision
  • undercommunicating the vision
  • failing to remove obstacles
  • failing to generate short-term wins
  • declaring victory too early
  • failing to anchor changes in culture

chapters.title: Chapter 8.2 — Power and Influence
chapters.content_html:
Power

Definition

Power is the ability to influence decisions, behaviour, or outcomes within an organization.

Explanation

Power is not automatically negative. The lecture emphasizes that power can be used for ethical or unethical ends. The morality lies in how influence is used, not in the mere fact that someone has power. Power also does not come only from formal hierarchy. Organizations contain both positional and personal sources of power.

Positional Power

Definition

Positional power is power that arises from a person's role in the organization.

Framework components

Main sources

  • formal authority
  • centrality
  • flexibility
  • visibility
  • relevance

Explanation

Why it matters

Positional power is useful in cases because it explains why some people have influence even when they are not at the very top of the hierarchy.

Formal Authority

Explanation

Power resulting directly from one's place in the organizational hierarchy.

Explanation

How to identify it in a case

If someone can approve, direct, assign, or formally overrule others because of their title or role, formal authority is involved.

Centrality

Explanation

Power that comes from being central in a communication or workflow network.

Explanation

How to identify it in a case

If many people depend on one person or unit to keep information, work, or coordination moving, centrality helps explain that influence.

Flexibility

Explanation

Power that comes from the ability to respond to uncertain situations, improvise, or solve problems when routines break down.

Explanation

How to identify it in a case

If a person becomes influential because they can act when rules are incomplete or conditions are changing, flexibility is an important source of power.

Visibility

Explanation

Power that comes from being seen, noticed, or connected to work that others consider important.

Explanation

How to identify it in a case

If someone gains influence because senior people see their work, or because they are highly visible in the organization, visibility is helping convert effort into power.

Relevance

Explanation

Power that comes from being tied to tasks, issues, or priorities the organization considers strategically important.

Explanation

How to identify it in a case

If a person's work sits close to a major priority such as safety, growth, restructuring, or a critical project, relevance helps explain their influence.

Personal Power

Definition

Personal power is power based on the individual rather than their formal role.

Framework components

Main sources

  • expertise
  • attractiveness
  • effort
  • legitimacy

Explanation

Why it matters

Personal power explains why people without high rank can still shape decisions, gain cooperation, or become influential in teams and organizations.

Expertise

Explanation

Power that comes from having knowledge or skill that other people depend on.

Explanation

How to identify it in a case

If others defer to a person because they know more, solve difficult problems, or hold critical specialized knowledge, expertise is operating.

Attractiveness

Explanation

Power that comes from personal appeal or the ability to make others want to affiliate, cooperate, or agree.

Explanation

How to identify it in a case

If people are drawn to someone, want to be associated with them, or are unusually willing to cooperate with them, attractiveness may be creating influence.

Effort

Explanation

Power that comes from persistence, initiative, and visible contribution.

Explanation

How to identify it in a case

If a person becomes influential because they consistently show initiative, take on difficult work, and make themselves useful, effort can become a source of power.

Legitimacy

Explanation

Power that comes from being seen as appropriate, credible, or entitled to influence a situation.

Explanation

How to identify it in a case

If others accept a person's input because it seems proper, reasonable, or justified that they should be involved, legitimacy is helping them influence outcomes.

Structural Holes and Brokerage

Explanation

A broker who connects otherwise unconnected groups can gain influence by moving knowledge across structural holes.

Explanation

Brokers gain power by linking disconnected parts of a network and controlling how information travels between them. This can increase both centrality and practical influence.

Explanation

Why it matters

If someone has no high title but is the only person connecting separate groups, brokerage helps explain why they can shape decisions.

Power vs Influence

Explanation

Power is the capacity or potential to affect outcomes. Influence is the actual process of changing others' attitudes or behaviour.

Explanation

Why it matters

A person can have power without using it effectively. An exam scenario may ask whether the problem is lack of power, poor use of power, or failure to convert power into influence.

Converting Power to Influence

Definition

Converting power to influence means turning potential capacity into actual cooperation, consent, or changed behaviour.

Explanation

Having power and successfully influencing others are not the same thing. Influence means securing the cooperation or consent of others in order to accomplish an objective. Power becomes influential only when it is recognized, applied, and accepted strongly enough to affect what people do.

The Path from Power Source to Influence Outcome

Explanation

The practical logic is:

  1. a person has a source of power
  2. that source becomes relevant in the situation
  3. the person uses an influence strategy
  4. others respond
  5. an influence outcome occurs

Explanation

Why it matters

This path helps with case analysis. The key question is not just "What power does this person have?" It is also "How are they trying to use it, and why is it working or failing?"

Three Influence Strategies

Explanation

Rational route

Uses logic, evidence, and clear arguments to shape decisions.

Explanation

How to recognize it

The person relies on facts, analysis, expertise, or structured reasoning to persuade others.

Explanation

Relational route

Uses trust, relationships, and social connection to gain cooperation.

Explanation

How to recognize it

The person gains support because others trust them, feel connected to them, or want to maintain the relationship.

Explanation

Political or exchange route

Uses bargaining, pressure, reciprocity, coalition building, or resource exchange to affect outcomes.

Explanation

How to recognize it

The person secures support by trading resources, building alliances, applying pressure, or using reciprocal obligations.

Explanation

Why it matters

The three routes should be distinguishable in scenarios. Rational influence is argument-based. Relational influence is trust-based. Political or exchange influence is resource- or coalition-based.

chapters.nav_title: Chapter 9 — Future of Work, Virtual Work, and AI & Work
chapters.content_html:
Future of Work

Definition

The future of work refers to ongoing changes in how people work, how organizations are designed, and how work is coordinated due to technology, remote work, automation, and labour market changes.

Framework components

Five game changers

  1. work moves from being long-term and time-based to temporary and task-based
  2. AI and automation may erode employment before fully replacing whole jobs
  3. AI may reduce the scarcity of knowledge workers and allow jobless growth in knowledge industries
  4. combined digital technologies may reduce the role of human intermediaries
  5. where people work and earn may not be where they live and spend

Explanation

Current challenges requiring evolving organization theory

  • globalization
  • ethics and social responsibility
  • speed of responsiveness
  • digital workplace
  • diversity

Explanation

Why it matters

The lecture uses these challenges to show why organization theory keeps evolving. Organizations face pressures that require new forms of coordination, communication, control, and design.

Virtual Work

Definition

Virtual work involves collaboration through digital communication technologies rather than shared physical space.

Explanation

Benefits of increasingly virtual teams

  • access to geographically distributed talent
  • flexibility
  • potentially lower facility cost
  • coordination across time and space

Explanation

Short-term effects

The lecture’s short-term design logic is tied closely to the rapid COVID-19 shift into remote work, which pushed organizations to adjust coordination and control quickly rather than redesign everything gradually.

  • more delegation
  • output-based control
  • more formalized processes

Explanation

Long-term effects

  • reduced interdependence
  • more pre-task coordination
  • more standardization
  • smaller teams
  • more individual objectives and rewards
  • more freelance and contract work

Related concepts

Personal vs Team Productivity

Employees may feel more productive individually because they face fewer interruptions and have more flexibility. At the same time, organizations may lose some team-level creativity or coordination capacity when collaboration becomes harder.

Explanation

Challenges of Virtual Teams

  • establishing norms
  • adoption of technology
  • meeting deadlines with reduced or absent face-to-face contact
  • communicating asynchronously
  • collaborating cross-culturally

Explanation

Computer-Mediated Communication

Digital communication tools shape how rich, fast, and interpretable interaction can be. Some messages are easy to send digitally, while others are harder to communicate well without richer media.

Explanation

Media richness / media capacity logic

Richer media are better suited to ambiguous, sensitive, or emotionally significant messages because they allow more cues, feedback, and clarification. Leaner media can work well for clearer, more routine, or more standardized communication.

Explanation

Why it matters

If a manager needs to communicate a routine update, a leaner medium may be sufficient. If the organization is announcing a controversial restructuring or trying to resolve confusion, richer communication becomes more appropriate.

AI and Work

Explanation

AI can improve:

  • knowledge synthesis
  • task planning
  • decision support in data-rich cases
  • content generation
  • code generation

AI risks include:

  • novelty loss
  • hallucination
  • dependency
  • weak causal reasoning
  • safety

AI also raises questions about expertise. It can improve execution efficiency while weakening how deeply people develop judgment, reasoning habits, and their own knowledge base if they rely on it uncritically.

Explanation

Why it matters

The key exam issue is not just whether AI is useful. It is whether organizations understand what kinds of work AI supports well, what it does poorly, and what new risks it creates for judgment and expertise.

Explanation

AI safety

Safety matters because AI outputs can be wrong, misleading, biased, or risky in ways that are not obvious at first glance. The course emphasis is that organizations should not treat fluent output as proof of reliability.

Explanation

Expertise and AI

AI can support execution and make some tasks faster, but it may also change the role of expertise. If people rely on AI without understanding the underlying reasoning, their own judgment and knowledge development can weaken over time.

Remote Work and Weak Ties

Explanation

Weak ties expose people to new information. Strong ties support deeper transfer of complex knowledge. Remote work may preserve strong ties while weakening weak ties, reducing exposure to new ideas.

chapters.title: Chapter 11.1 — Ethics and Talent Management
chapters.content_html:
Ethics

Definition

Ethics is the code of moral principles and values that governs the behaviour of a person or group with respect to what is right or wrong.

Explanation

Ethics matters in organizations because decisions affect employees, customers, the public, and the environment. The lecture also emphasizes engineering ethics and responsibilities toward safety, competence, fairness, and the public interest.

Engineering Ethics

Framework components

Core themes

  • protect public safety, health, and welfare
  • work within competence
  • avoid conflicts of interest
  • maintain competence
  • act with integrity and fairness
  • communicate consequences of ignored engineering decisions
  • report illegal or unethical practices
  • consider societal and environmental consequences

Explanation

These duties emphasize public welfare, competence, integrity, disclosure, fairness, and respect. The main exam point is that engineering ethics is not only about private personal values. It creates professional obligations that shape organizational decision-making.

Ethics as a Value

Explanation

Ethical values are among the most important organizational values because they set standards for what is considered good or bad conduct and decision making.

Forces That Shape Managerial Ethics

Explanation

The lecture's core distinctions are:

  • personal ethics
  • organizational culture
  • organizational systems and processes
  • external stakeholders

Personal Ethics

Explanation

Personal ethics refers to the individual's own moral principles and values.

Explanation

Why it matters

Managers do not enter organizations as blank slates. Their own beliefs shape how they interpret dilemmas, obligations, and acceptable behaviour.

Organizational Culture

Explanation

Organizational culture shapes what people see as normal, rewarded, tolerated, or discouraged.

Explanation

Why it matters

Even when people know what is right, culture can either support ethical action or pressure people toward silence and compromise.

Organizational Systems and Processes

Explanation

Organizational systems and processes include rewards, controls, reporting systems, policies, and decision routines.

Explanation

Why it matters

An organization can hire ethical individuals and still encourage unethical behaviour if its systems reward concealment, short-termism, or rule avoidance.

External Stakeholders

Explanation

External stakeholders include customers, regulators, professional bodies, communities, and other outside groups that shape expectations about acceptable behaviour.

Explanation

Why it matters

Ethics is not determined only inside the firm. External pressure and accountability also shape what managers see as legitimate or necessary.

Why Employee Treatment Matters

Explanation

Treating employees ethically is morally important, but it is also often linked to commitment, performance, and customer outcomes. The lecture explicitly connects ethical employee treatment to stronger attachment and better organizational functioning.

Institutionalizing Ethics

Explanation

Organizations can make ethics part of daily work rather than leaving it at the level of abstract values.

Explanation

This can include

  • bringing ethics formally into business life
  • using formal codes and policy at high management levels
  • integrating ethics into daily decision-making and work practices

Explanation

Why it matters

An ethics code by itself is not enough if the organization does not build ethics into routines, incentives, and decisions.

Ethically-Oriented Culture

Explanation

An ethically-oriented culture makes values, goals, purposes, and beliefs about ethics explicit.

It also depends on leaders acting as role models, on authority relationships being designed carefully, and on responsibility for consequences being assigned clearly.

Organizational Commitment

Explanation

Organizational commitment is the relative strength of an individual's identification with and involvement in the organization.

Explanation

Factors Influencing Commitment

  1. Visibility — ethical behaviour becomes more committing when it is observable to others
  2. Explicitness — expected behaviour is clearly stated and difficult to deny or ignore
  3. Volition — people feel personal responsibility and choice in following the rules

Explanation

Why it matters

These factors matter because employees are more likely to internalize ethical expectations when the expectations are visible, explicit, and tied to personal responsibility.

Talent Management

Definition

Talent management is the system used to attract, develop, motivate, retain, and manage employees.

Explanation

In this chapter, talent management matters because organizations shape behaviour not only through values, but also through who they hire, how they train people, how they evaluate them, and what they reward. Talent-management systems therefore help translate ethics into everyday organizational practice.

Explanation

Why it matters

If selection, development, evaluation, and rewards are misaligned with ethical values, the organization can undermine its own ethics architecture.
